body.text: Facts won over fantasy when former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon was convicted of double murder
The murder trial of Beau Lamarre-Condon has been an emotional and horrific saga in which a then-police officer, allegedly driven by jealous vengeance, murdered two young men.
Warning: This story contains content that may disturb some readers.
As the prosecution put it in closing, "his wounded pride had driven him to a far darker plan for revenge".
Jesse Baird rejected him, so he took his life, and that of Luke Davies who was "eliminated as a witness" on 19 February 2024.
Lamarre-Condon claimed he and Baird were more romantically involved than in reality, and in truth, he was nothing more than a casual fling.
A former celebrity-chaser, he was infatuated with Baird, and within months of their first meeting in late 2022, had hacked and tampered with Baird's phone.
For the victim's loved ones, this is the conclusion of a drawn-out ordeal.
From the killings to the days in which Lamarre-Condon drove the bodies around Sydney in a van, and then Bungonia, to his switching of lawyers and his delays in entering a plea.
Then, in November this year, his lengthy testimony began. It was so laden with embellishments that it had some jurors stifling laughter and shaking their heads in the court room.
He was a "proven and persistent liar", the prosecution told the jury.
But nothing will end the pain for both Baird's and Davies's family and friends who sat in the public gallery.
Some collapsed in the witness stand as they recalled Baird's fear of a policeman who had access to a gun.
They did this as Lamarre-Condon played the victim.

On the second day of his testimony he clutched rosary beads as he cried over himself, claiming it was he who was planning to take his own life, in a way that would not cause trauma to others, and that he was bullied by other police officers.

But when protecting himself from a barrage of prosecution questions, he turned off the tears, recounting specific dates and certain events with laser-like precision, and borrowing heavily from evidence already heard.
In his evidence he admitted to varying degrees of deceit: "an unintentional lie" or a "white lie".
He said taking an Uber Eats rider's uniform and helmet from a motorbike was not stealing.
He told the court that if he got caught he would just "explain myself and laugh about it".
The former police officer believed snooping through Baird's phone and blocking other male contacts, several times, was OK.

To Lamarre-Condon breaking into Baird's house at night and stealing his phone while he slept — so he could check whether Baird was seeing other men — when he could have simply asked him, was perfectly reasonable.
Forcing a friend to send Baird a 1,600-word message he wrote, claiming he had cancer when he did not, made sense to him.
Science trumps fiction
But for all his twisted explanations, he missed something more fundamental — the facts.

The guilty verdict is a testament to the meticulous care of the NSW Police forensic team, and the officer in charge of the investigation, Detective Sasha Pinazza, who was a calm presence in the court room and had earlier persuaded him to reveal the location of the bodies in 2024.
The forensic evidence prevailed over Lamarre-Condon's fantasy world. He went for the drama, not the science.
Lamarre-Condon claimed he initially shot Baird in the shoulder, and the second shot accidentally hit him in the head.
The evidence proved Baird was shot in the neck from behind and almost vertically through the head, while he lay on the floor.
Lamarre-Condon claimed Davies accidentally shot himself in a struggle that took place in the hallway outside the bedroom door.
The evidence proved Lamarre-Condon shot Davies through that bedroom door.
He had covered up the bullet hole with a plastic hook, only for the police to find it when they re-examined the door in July this year.
Perhaps the most compelling piece of evidence was a tiny piece of metadata.
Lamarre-Condon's timeline did not add up.
In his own evidence the former policeman claimed that he rummaged through boxes after entering the front door. That took one minute.
He claimed he then hid upstairs in the house, for a couple of minutes.
The prosecution told the court it took about four seconds to kill Baird, and Davies was killed 51 seconds later.
The jury ultimately saw through the illusion and Lamarre-Condon was proven to be bad at maths, a bad liar, or, both.
In the aftermath there will likely be further questions about whether Lamarre-Condon was ever a good fit for the police force.
Throughout his career he appeared more interested in cashing up on extra shifts to watch concerts, while running a bikini business on the side, and reselling Hermes handbags he bought in Paris.
Now Lamarre-Condon's police cosplay as an honourable officer of the law is over. He's a convicted murderer.
